messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Tane

Tane was forty-seven when the accident happened. He had been working in community organizing for over a decade by then, running youth outreach programs in South Auckland, and he was good at the work—the kind of man who showed up, who listened, who made young people feel seen. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, he was driving a van full of teenagers back from a field trip to a local environmental center. The rain had come down hard that morning, and the roads were still slick. He remembered the sky clearing. He remembered a radio announcement. Then there was nothing—a gap like someone had taken scissors to the film of his life. When consciousness returned, he was upside down, metal screaming, the smell of fuel and something else, something like copper. A boy was crying. Tane's right leg was pinned. The next clear image was a police officer's face through the broken window, then the sound of the jaws of life, then pain so sharp it seemed to split him open. Three teenagers had been injured. None had died. Tane had spent eight weeks in hospital.

The physical recovery took months. The psychological one, he had come to understand, might never finish. It was now sixteen years later, and Tane still could not account for the middle section of the accident—the moment of impact itself remained sealed off, inaccessible. He knew intellectually what must have happened: the van had hydroplaned, crossed the centerline, struck a utility vehicle head-on. But he could not access the sensory reality of it, could not find the words to describe even what he did remember. When he tried to talk about it in those early years, his mouth would open and close like a fish pulled from water. Eventually he stopped trying.

What he could not stop were the thoughts. They arrived unbidden and unwelcome—images of the teenagers' faces, scenarios in which the outcome had been different, darker. The thoughts felt like intrusions, like something pressing against his skull from the inside. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that the accident had been his fault. He had been driving. He had made the decision to take that route. He had not anticipated the rain. The logic was circular and airtight: if he had acted differently—left earlier, chosen a different road, driven slower—those young people would not have been in danger. The fact that they had survived did not absolve him; it only meant he had been lucky, and luck was not the same as innocence.

Over the years, Tane had constructed a careful architecture of avoidance. He no longer drove. He took the bus, walked, or accepted rides from colleagues. He stopped attending community events where police or security personnel might be present in uniform; the sight of that blue or black fabric, the badge and belt, sent his heart into a gallop and made his palms sweat uncontrollably. His body, he had come to feel, was a traitor—it reacted as if danger were imminent even when he sat safely in his living room. Sometimes his leg would twitch involuntarily, or his chest would tighten, and he would think: *there is nothing happening, but my body does not believe that*. The disconnect was profound. He felt dead inside, as though the part of him that could feel joy or connection had been severed in that moment of impact and had never regenerated.

Most difficult was his response to anger in others. When a colleague raised their voice in a meeting, even with legitimate frustration about a funding delay, Tane's nervous system would flood with alarm. His hands would shake. He would excuse himself. Over time, he began avoiding meetings where conflict might arise, then avoiding colleagues who seemed prone to intensity, then avoiding the office altogether. His supervisor had gently suggested he might consider part-time work. The irony was not lost on him: a man whose life's work was community building had become increasingly isolated, increasingly unreachable.

At sixty-three, Tane sat in his small apartment in Wellington, where he had moved after retiring early, and admitted to himself that something had to change. The isolation was complete now. The unwanted thoughts had become louder. His body's betrayals had become more frequent. He had finally called a therapist because he could no longer live inside the architecture he had built. He was afraid that talking about it would make it real in a way that silence had prevented. But he was more afraid of spending the rest of his life as a ghost in his own life—numb, trapped, unable to move toward anything or anyone.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: The vignette states Tane was 47 when the accident occurred 16 years ago, making him 63 at present, which matches the patient's current age. However, the vignette explicitly establishes the accident occurred when Tane was 47, not reflecting the patient's actual current age of 63 as the trauma occurrence point. The vignette does correctly show Tane at 63 in the present timeline, but this creates an internal inconsistency: the patient's age (63) appears to be the current age in the vignette, yet the trauma type and all symptom descriptions reference an accident from 16 years prior when he was 47. While the final age is correct, the narrative structure makes the age context ambiguous relative to when the trauma occurred versus the patient's reported current state.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Tane was forty-seven when the accident happened. He had been working in community organizing for over a decade by then, running youth outreach programs in South Auckland, and he was good at the work—the kind of man who showed up, who listened, who made young people feel seen. The next clear image was a police officer's face through the broken window, then the sound of the jaws of life, then pain so sharp it seemed to split him open. Three teenagers had been injured. None had died. Tane had spent eight weeks in hospital. Now, at sixty-three, sixteen years had passed since that Tuesday, and the distance of time had done almost nothing to dull the weight of what he carried.

The physical recovery had taken months. The psychological one, he had come to understand, might never finish. The middle section of the accident—the moment of impact itself—remained sealed off, inaccessible. He knew intellectually what must have happened: the van had hydroplaned, crossed the centerline, struck a utility vehicle head-on. But he could not access the sensory reality of it, could not find the words to describe even what he did remember. When he tried to talk about it in those early years, his mouth would open and close like a fish pulled from water. Eventually he stopped trying. What he could not stop were the thoughts. They arrived unbidden and unwelcome—images of the teenagers' faces, scenarios in which the outcome had been different, darker. The thoughts felt like intrusions, like something pressing against his skull from the inside. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that the accident had been his fault. He had been driving. He had made the decision to take that route. He had not anticipated the rain. The logic was circular and airtight: if he had acted differently—left earlier, chosen a different road, driven slower—those young people would not have been in danger. The fact that they had survived did not absolve him; it only meant he had been lucky, and luck was not the same as innocence.

Over the years, Tane had constructed a careful architecture of avoidance that had slowly contracted the boundaries of his life. He no longer drove; the moment he sat behind a steering wheel, his hands would begin to shake uncontrollably, and his vision would narrow as though the world were closing in. He took the bus, walked, or accepted rides from colleagues, though fewer colleagues remained willing to offer them as he became less present at work. He stopped attending community events where police or security personnel might be present in uniform; the sight of that blue or black fabric, the badge and belt, sent his heart into a gallop and made his palms sweat in a way he could not control. His body, he had come to feel, was a traitor—it reacted as if danger were imminent even when he sat safely in his living room. Sometimes his leg would twitch involuntarily, or his chest would tighten, and he would think: *there is nothing happening, but my body does not believe that*. The disconnect was profound. He felt dead inside, as though the part of him that could feel joy or connection had been severed in that moment of impact and had never regenerated. He experienced a persistent numbness that made even his favorite foods taste like cardboard, made conversations feel like he was speaking through thick glass.

Most difficult was his response to anger in others. When a colleague raised their voice in a meeting, even with legitimate frustration about a funding delay, Tane's nervous system would flood with alarm. His hands would shake. He would excuse himself. Over time, he began avoiding meetings where conflict might arise, then avoiding colleagues who seemed prone to intensity, then avoiding the office altogether. His supervisor had gently suggested he might consider part-time work, then eventually part-time had become a medical leave, then early retirement. The irony was not lost on him: a man whose life's work was community building had become increasingly isolated, increasingly unreachable. When he moved to Wellington at fifty-five, telling himself it was for a fresh start, it was really to remove himself entirely from the world he had built.

At sixty-three, Tane sat in his small apartment in Wellington, where the light came in gray through the windows overlooking the harbor, and admitted to himself that something had to change. The isolation was complete now. The unwanted thoughts had become louder, more vivid, arriving with a clarity that felt almost hallucinatory—he could see the teenagers' faces, could hear the sound of metal tearing. His body's betrayals had become more frequent and more severe; sometimes his heart would race for hours with no trigger he could identify. He had finally called a therapist because he could no longer live inside the architecture he had built. He was afraid that talking about it would make it real in a way that silence had prevented, that speaking the details aloud would somehow unlock the sealed-off moment of impact and flood him with sensations he was not sure he could survive. But he was more afraid of spending the rest of his life as a ghost in his own life—numb, trapped, unable to move toward anything or anyone. At sixty-three, he was running out of time to become a person again.
